children.text: What does it mean when a child is born in a country like the US, Canada, Australia, or the UK? Does this mean the child automatically becomes a citizen of that country and receives all the corresponding rights? In a world where emigration and travel are increasingly common, it's important to know how different countries' laws regulate citizenship by birth.

In this blog, we take a detailed look at how various countries regulate the acquisition of citizenship by birth. Where citizenship is granted automatically, and where additional conditions need to be met.
It often happens that non-citizen parents of Canada have a child born in Canada. In such cases, a child born in Canada is granted many advantages, first among them citizenship.

Under Canadian law, any child born on the country's territory automatically becomes a Canadian citizen, regardless of their parents' immigration status. The citizen child is granted a Canadian passport, one of the strongest documents in the world, allowing its holder to travel visa-free to 113 countries.
A Canadian citizen child has the right to:
Live, work, and study in Canada without restriction for their entire life;
In the future, sponsor their own parents to move to Canada, to obtain residency and later citizenship;
Benefit from state services, such as free or accessible healthcare, enrollment in the education system, and social support;
Upon reaching adulthood, participate in elections and benefit from legal protection mechanisms.
A child born in the US is granted many advantages, including automatic citizenship.

Under US federal law, any child born on US territory automatically becomes a citizen of the country, regardless of their parents' immigration status. Accordingly, the child receives a US passport, allowing visa-free travel to 111 countries. A child who is a US citizen also enjoys the protection of the US government anywhere in the world.
A citizen born in the US enjoys all the same social, economic, and political rights as other American citizens. They have the right to:
Receive secondary and higher education;
Access government financial assistance, including student loans and grants;
Work in the US without any immigration restrictions.
From a political standpoint, an American citizen has the right to:
Participate in elections upon reaching adulthood;
And after the age of 21, sponsor their family members so they can move to live in the US, obtain residency, and later citizenship.
It's particularly worth noting that the right to benefit from social programs is only granted to the child if they physically reside within US territory.
US law does not prohibit dual citizenship. In such cases, the US government considers the person solely as an American citizen, even if they also hold citizenship of another country.
Unlike many other countries, a child born in Australia does not automatically receive citizen status unless at least one of their parents is an Australian citizen or permanent resident.

A child receives Australian citizenship only if, at the time of birth, one or both parents are Australian citizens or permanent residents. In such cases, the child automatically becomes an Australian citizen at birth.

If the child's parents do not hold Australian citizenship or permanent resident status, but the child lives permanently in Australia from birth until age 10, then the child automatically acquires Australian citizenship at age 10, regardless of the parents' immigration status.

There are also cases where the parents are neither citizens nor residents. In such cases, the child's immigration status depends on the type of visa the parents hold. For example, if the parents are in the country on a temporary visa, the child will also receive the same type of visa.
When a child becomes an Australian citizen, they are granted full citizen rights, including:
The right to obtain an Australian passport;
The right to vote in elections (upon reaching adulthood);
The right to receive social benefits, including healthcare programs;
The right to education at every level;
The unrestricted right to live, study, and work in Australia.

If the child of a foreign national is born in Finland, they will not receive Finnish citizenship at birth. However, the child's data is registered in Finland's population information system, and they are assigned a personal identity number.
A foreign national's child born in Finland receives Finnish citizenship only if, at the time of birth, their mother or father holds Finnish citizenship.

There's also an exception: if neither of the child's parents holds Finnish citizenship, and the child cannot obtain citizenship of another country through their parent, then in such a case, the child is granted Finnish citizen status.

A child born in the UK can obtain citizenship if, at the time of birth, at least one parent was a British citizen or held permanent resident status. In such cases, the child automatically becomes a British citizen and can apply for a British passport.

If, at the time of birth, neither of the child's parents was a British citizen or permanent resident, but the child has lived in the UK continuously for 10 years, without spending more than 90 days outside the country's borders during that period, they can obtain citizenship through registration.

For this purpose, a special form, "Form T," is completed, after which an appointment is scheduled at an Application Centre, where the child's biometric data, fingerprints, and photo are collected. Along with the application, a birth certificate and other documents must be submitted confirming that the applicant lived continuously in the UK for 10 years.
Being born in Ireland does not automatically mean receiving citizenship, nor does it grant the child the right to permanent residence.
Under Irish law, a child born on the country's territory becomes an Irish citizen only under certain conditions.

If the child's parents are citizens of another country and neither holds Irish or EU citizenship, the child does not receive citizenship by birth. In this case, the child is only granted temporary residency, depending on the type of the parent's visa or residence status.

The child will be able to apply for citizenship in the future only if certain conditions are met - for example, when the parent has legally resided in Ireland for at least 3 years before the child's birth.

If one of the child's parents is an Irish or EU citizen, then the child becomes an Irish citizen at birth and enjoys all corresponding rights, including the right to residence, education, healthcare, and social support.
